item.title: My local LLM didn't replace my $20 Claude subscription, it replaced everything I was never comfortable sending to the cloud
item.itunes:title: My local LLM didn't replace my $20 Claude subscription, it replaced everything I was never comfortable sending to the cloud
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Over the past couple of months, I've experimented with the idea of reducing my dependence on cloud-based AI services for various reasons. For one, they can be expensive. For another, my personal and professional workflows involve a lot of information that I couldn't reasonably trust a cloud service with.

My experiments have, indeed, seen relative success in terms of cost savings. I've talked about how using a hybrid approach involving switching between capable local coding models in developer workflows can cut cloud AI spending by up to 50%, and I have pocketed the savings from utilizing this method.

And yet, I still wouldn't vouch for a total local-only approach because of the obvious trade-offs associated with capability. That's why I've taken to reserving my cloud models for the work that needs them, while anything more sensitive for a cloud server can stay with my local LLM.

My local LLM offers zero data retention by default

I can do my taxes, look at health records, and dump my bank statements

The most liberating aspect about running my local model on my own machine isn't the full control that I have over the model's reasoning, size, or capability (although I've come to appreciate all three), but it's the fact that I can go to bed every night knowing that my data has never left my PC. My prompts go into llama.cpp's web interface, the response comes back, and there's no trail, no monitoring, and no flags that give license to a third party to audit my conversations.

Without that anxiety, there's a surprising lot of things that I can put in front of my model. I can hand it a year of bank statements and ask it to tag every subscription service I've forgotten about, I can paste a lab report and query what the acronyms mean before I see a doctor, or dump my tax spreadsheet and have it flag the deductions that I missed. A growing number of users have found such use cases for local LLMs, and a growing number have come to appreciate the liberty.

With local AI, my prompts go into llama.cpp's web interface, the response comes back, and there's no trail, no monitoring, and no flags that give license to a third party to audit my conversations.

Trying to self-host LLMs made me realize local AI has a friction problem, not a quality problem

Think of it as the Linux desktop problem, all over again

30
By  Samarveer Singh

No major cloud AI provider offers ZDR to everyday customers

Which meant my chats and my data sat on their servers, by default

Out of the three major cloud AI service providers, including Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, none offer zero data retention by default, and consumer plans don't offer it at all.

On Anthropic, ZDR is an opt-in arrangement for enterprise, Claude Platform, and API customers who negotiate it with the sales team on a per-organization basis. Even then, inputs and outputs can be retained for up to two years if Claude's automated trust and safety systems flag a session. For consumers like myself paying $20 for Claude Pro, there simply isn't an option for this at all.

Google, on the other hand, saves Gemini chats to Gemini Apps Activity for 18 months as default, and human reviewers can read anonymized snippets through this. And if you're thinking that simply turning activity off would solve the problem, then you're just as wrong as I initially was. Google still holds conversations for 72 hours for monitoring before dropping them. On the Gemini developer API, prompts persist in the abuse logs for a default of 55 days.

On OpenAI's platform, ChatGPT Free, Plus, and Pro, save chats indefinitely until you manually delete them, and conversations may feed training unless you turn it off. Though ZDR exists on the API, it only exists for approved customers, and it never applies to ChatGPT itself.

I stopped paying for ChatGPT after putting my local LLM on Tailscale

My phone finally reaches my home server the same way it reaches ChatGPT.

13
By  Korbin Brown

Cloud models have developed a tier problem lately

You can use them for free, but the best models start at $20

A question any reasonable user would ask going through all of this is, "Why not just use the free tiers of cloud models?", and that is a question that I've asked myself time and again. The most recent problem is the fact that capability is being gatekept behind a paywall, and lately it seems that the gates have been closing fast this year, which has become a pattern amongst cloud AI service providers.

On Claude's free plan, you don't get access to any Opus or Fable models at all. These are the models a user reaches for to handle hard reasoning, complex app development, or long-document work. Free users only get access to Sonnet or Haiku, which, while capable, aren't at the top of the stack.

Google recently made this argument for me. On October 9, it revoked free users' access to Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro, leaving the free tier with Gemini 3.5 Flash-lite, which is the smallest model in the family. Even the users paying $4.99 a month lost access to Pro, which now costs $19.99 through the AI Pro plan. This trend has led to the rise of a serious capability divide between users, which means that paying users get access to a different standard of service entirely, which wasn't the case a few months ago.

Unlike cloud services where the best models are kept away until you pay, you get the full capability of a local model right when it's loaded into your VRAM. That gives me more of a reason to always keep a 27B model file on my desktop.

Unlike cloud services where the best models are kept away until you pay, you get the full capability of a local model right when it's loaded into your VRAM.

I'm not done with cloud AI, but I have a safer way to use AI after all

One of the most concerning aspects of opening up my sensitive data to cloud models is guessing what it's being used for, what it's training, and where it can show up following an adverse event. I've previously talked about how a normal user over years shares and dumps far more information on the AI platform of their choice than they ever would on a search engine or an online forum, which makes them more vulnerable as their dependence rises.

It also has to be taken into account that AI isn't profitable yet, and it makes one wonder how major providers will get there. OpenAI recently rolled out ads to users on Free and Go tiers, and keeping personal information away from advertisers becomes an act of trusting a corporation and that its policy won't change with time. A local model running on my own PC is the only option right now where that level of trust isn't necessary.

item.title: Your Windows laptop has crucial security settings that you're probably ignoring
item.itunes:title: Your Windows laptop has crucial security settings that you're probably ignoring
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Unlike your desktop, your laptop is exposed to several threat vectors simply because it leaves the safety of your home, giving attackers many more ways to steal it or compromise your data. That's not to say that you shouldn't enable basic security settings on your desktop, but they become way more critical on your Windows laptop.

While some security settings are enabled by default on a new Windows 11 installation, you have to manually opt in to others. By enabling them, you effectively make it harder for attackers to threaten or steal your data even if they gain control of your machine. They'll also help if someone intends to mess with your data or settings when your laptop is unattended.

Your motherboard's old debug header is still listening, and it's an unpatched security risk

A cheap logic board and a few minutes are all one needs to steal your data

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Controlled folder access

Prevent unauthorized data encryption and deletion

I'm assuming your laptop doubles up as your work machine and possibly stores some of your financial information, too. Even if it doesn't leave the house, it can still get caught up in a ransomware attack. Attackers routinely use unassuming entry points like phishing emails, malicious websites, and pirated media to inject ransomware into thousands of machines. Your unprotected folders can be held for ransom before you know what happened.

Although Windows Security protects against ransomware and other types of security attacks, enabling Controlled folder access (CFA) can provide your data with an additional layer of protection. Even if a new ransomware strain bypasses the default security controls, CFA will prevent it from modifying your files, since it will not have the necessary permissions. CFA will block the attacks and notify you of the same.

It also protects critical boot sectors from boot-level ransomware, so attackers can't lock you out of the entire OS. You can toggle CFA on by navigating to Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage ransomware protection, or simply searching for it in the search bar. By default, CFA protects folders like Documents, Pictures, Music, and Videos, but you can add any other folder you want to protect.

7 ways your Windows PC can get hacked (And what you can do about it)

Your Windows PC is more vulnerable than you think.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Dynamic lock

Automatically lock your device when you walk away

If you aren't in the habit of manually locking your laptop in a library or café when walking away for a glass of water or a bio break, anyone can gain access to your unattended device. It doesn't have to be a determined attacker after your sensitive data. It could simply be a prying stranger or even a friend intent on causing mischief. Your screen lock settings might take too long to lock your laptop, so enabling Dynamic lock can provide a backup layer of protection.

Enabling it requires pairing your laptop with your smartphone, so that Windows can detect when you've left your device unattended. It monitors the Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) of your phone's Bluetooth connection, waiting for it to drop below a certain threshold. It waits for about 30 to 60 seconds before locking your laptop, preventing unauthorized access. You can find Dynamic lock at Settings > Account > Sign-in options > Dynamic lock.

Although the physical environment around the laptop can influence the distance needed to trigger the lock, this is still a useful setting to enable. Note that someone can still access your device within the 30-to-60-second grace period.

5 obscure Windows tools I use that do one thing incredibly well

I use these obscure tools on Windows because they do what they are designed for.

1
By  Brian Burgess

Device encryption

Hide your data from prying eyes

Most new Windows laptops have device encryption enabled by default, but you may have disabled BitLocker on your laptop for fear of a performance penalty. However, the benefits of BitLocker easily outweigh any negligible performance impact it might have on a modern laptop. Features like CFA can protect your data from unauthorized modification, but Full Disk Encryption (FDE) protects your entire drive.

Without the decryption key, nobody can access the data on your drive. If an attacker removes your hard drive or SSD from the laptop and plugs it into another computer, they can't make sense of the data without the BitLocker Recovery key. You can enable device encryption at Settings > Privacy & security > Device encryption.

Attackers can obviously erase a stolen drive or laptop and sell it to make some cash, but FDE ensures your data remains safe from unauthorized access.

A new Windows 11 BitLocker bypass only needs a USB stick, and the researcher thinks it's a backdoor

Apparently, not even TPM+PIN is safe from YellowKey.

3
By  Adam Conway

Tamper Protection

Who will guard the guards?

Each of the settings above involves setting up an additional security layer to protect your data, but what if someone disables the said security controls themselves? Malware is sophisticated enough to take control of your laptop by slowly dismantling your security settings. All of your carefully curated security features will do nothing if malware manages to disable them.

This is why enabling Tamper Protection is essential, not just on laptops but even on desktops. This feature stops apps and processes from making any changes to your machine's security infrastructure. While you, as an administrator, can still tweak your security settings, any app pr process is blocked. You can toggle Tamper Protection on at Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings (under Virus & threat protection settings).

4 things I do on a new Windows PC to tighten my security

Most PCs don't get hacked, they get neglected.

1
By  Marshall Gunnell

Enable these security settings on a new Windows laptop

Microsoft's built-in security settings have gotten fairly robust over time, so much so that many users don't use third-party protection at all. When you're setting up a new laptop, many of these settings are pre-enabled, but you still need to turn others on. These settings will protect your laptop both inside and outside your house by preventing attackers from gaining unauthorized access or disabling the security features themselves.

7 ways your Windows PC can get hacked (And what you can do about it)

Your Windows PC is more vulnerable than you think.

Dynamic lock

Automatically lock your device when you walk away

If you aren't in the habit of manually locking your laptop in a library or café when walking away for a glass of water or a bio break, anyone can gain access to your unattended device. Most PCs don't get hacked, they get neglected.

item.title: I turned off 2.4GHz Wi-Fi on my primary SSID, and household smart devices stopped dropping offline
item.itunes:title: I turned off 2.4GHz Wi-Fi on my primary SSID, and household smart devices stopped dropping offline
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The frustration of modern wireless network management is that your high-end Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 7 router can broadcast a single unified SSID across 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz (assuming your smart devices and modern laptops will handle it gracefully). However, instead of stability, this will cause your static smart plug, security cameras, and bulbs to constantly lose connection, stutter, or fail to respond because the network tries to force modern roaming logic onto single-band microcontrollers.

You can break the cycle of constant power cycling with hard network segmentation: remove 2.4GHz from your primary roaming SSID and dedicate a clean, isolated 2.4GHz-only network exclusively to your IoT gear. Dual-band convenience features are a trap for most power users. By turning off 2.4GHz on your primary SSID, you remove client confusion, protect your high-speed airtime, and bring permanent stability to your smart home.

Stop using Wi-Fi for your smart home

You're crippling your own internet speeds

25
By  Jasmine Mannan

Why do IoT devices cause so many issues?

The chips are not made for 5GHz

Combined SSIDs can confuse a lot of IoT clients. This is because modern client steering clashes with legacy 2.4GHz microcontrollers.

Many IoT devices use legacy 2.4GHz microcontroller chips to keep costs and power consumption down. When a router broadcasts 2.4GHz and 5GHz under the same SSID, devices constantly evaluate signal metrics to decide where to connect (even though your IoT devices aren't compatible with the 5GHz band).

Low-power IoT Wi-Fi chips, often running stripped-down or RTOS firmware, can struggle with aggressive roaming algorithms. The router constantly tries to steer or probe them, or the device misinterprets band parameters, resulting in sudden dropouts and ghost offline states in your smart home dashboard.

How to separate your network

You'll gain back performance

This means stripping 2.4GHz from your main SSID can create much better network hygiene. Clean band segregation is the gold standard for power users with a large smart home. This relies on deterministic client binding, forcing your phones, laptops, tablets, and any other primary devices to live exclusively on 5GHz/6GHz. This ensures that they never waste cycles negotiating with slow legacy bands that they don't need to. This, of course, relies on all your primary devices being compatible with 5GHz, which should be the case as long as you're not running any legacy devices.

This gives you airtime fairness, since 2.4GHz operates on wide-open, heavily congested channels prone to interference from Bluetooth, microwaves, and neighbor networks. Keeping your high-speed traffic off of 2.4GHz prevents low-bit-rate IoT beacon frames from choking your primary network throughput.

To begin, audit your wireless configuration before you start. Log into your router or access point controller and inspect your primary wireless profiles. Then disable 2.4GHz on the main profile. To do this, uncheck the 2.4GHz radio on your high-speed primary SSID, leaving only 5GHz. If you have 6GHz available, leave that on as well.

Keeping these active on your primary SSID lets all your primary daily drivers use them. Next, create a dedicated IoT SSID by setting up a separate 2.4GHz-only network for your smart home devices. You can name it something like home_iot_2.4 so it's easy to differentiate between them. By connecting all your smart devices to it, you lock them into a stable, non-roaming environment. When you re-pair and verify, you should watch your automation dropouts disappear.

You might face some issues

But they're rectifiable

When you migrate to this networking method, you may encounter hurdles, and these provisioning headaches can be frustrating.

The first is the companion app onboarding barrier. Many modern smart home setup apps, like Tuya, Matter, or even proprietary third-party apps, require your smartphone to be on the same band during initial pairing to push credentials. If your phone is locked to 5GHz or 6GHz, the setup wizard fails.

To fix this, you can use a temporary bridge workaround with temporary SSID provisioning, guest networks, or by temporarily disabling 5GHz during initial pairing before pairing devices securely to your dedicated 2.4GHz-only IoT SSID.

Don't leave your router on its default settings

They might not be the best for your network

Consumer routers try to automate everything in order to make setup easier for non-technical users. While this is great for the most part, in dense smart homes and for power users, that automation breeds instability. Taking manual control of your frequency bands is the ultimate cure for an erratic network. Remove 2.4GHz from your main SSID today. Build a dedicated home automation lane and enjoy a smart home that finally stays online.

item.title: I stopped using Notion, Obsidian, and Google Keep after finding this underrated alternative
item.itunes:title: I stopped using Notion, Obsidian, and Google Keep after finding this underrated alternative
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I regularly start my days without a cup of coffee or breakfast. Sure, that means I'll probably have a raging migraine for the rest of the day, but it's become a routine more often than I'd like to admit. You're probably wondering what my questionable breakfast habits have to do with an article about note-taking apps. Well, while I might be terrible at maintaining even the most basic routines, there's one habit I've managed to stick to religiously: taking notes.

I won't start a single morning without opening some sort of note-taking app. The problem, though, is that I've never been able to settle on a single app for doing so. Notion has been my go-to for organizing every aspect of my life for years, Obsidian is excellent for connecting ideas and managing research, and Google Keep is unmatched for jotting down quick thoughts. While each app serves its purpose, constantly jumping between three different platforms has become a headache of its own. So, I finally replaced all three with a single app.

AFFiNE is the all-in-one note-taking app I needed

My notes finally have a single home

AFFiNE (yes, it's intentionally spelled that way) is an open-source, local-first note-taking and knowledge management app that combines note-taking, databases, and an infinite whiteboard into a single workspace. My colleagues here at XDA have constantly praised the tool, and Nolen even went ahead and described it as a bit like Obsidian, Notion, Miro, and NotebookLM combined in a minimalist package.

The tool is available on Windows, macOS, and Linux as a desktop application, and you can also access it directly through your browser without downloading anything. There are mobile apps for iOS and Android, too. If you'd rather have complete control over where your data lives, AFFiNE also supports self-hosting through Docker Compose. Personally, though, that's not something I'd prefer, since I just don't have the hardware or patience to maintain a self-hosted setup when the desktop app works perfectly fine on its own.

It makes note-taking ridiculously easy

I didn't sign up for a course in note-taking

While Google Keep is fairly easy to use and a toddler could practically learn their way around the tool, Notion and Obsidian are a completely different story. Both of these tools come with a much steeper learning curve. I've spent hours upon hours setting up Notion databases and trying to figure out what even relations and rollups are supposed to do. Obsidian hasn't been much easier, either. Between getting used to Markdown, manually linking notes together to build a useful knowledge graph, and going down endless rabbit holes trying to find the right plugins, I've probably spent more time customizing my workspace than actually taking notes.

AFFiNE, though, is a breath of fresh air. Despite having an impressive number of features packed into one app, it's surprisingly easy to get the hang of. If you've used Notion before, the interface should feel immediately familiar. There's a sidebar on the left for navigating between your notes, and a clean, uncluttered editor that lets you get straight to writing. You don't need to spend hours setting up databases, configuring plugins, or learning Markdown syntax to get started.

I tried replacing Notion with Obsidian as my main note-taking app and here’s how it went

The truth about switching from Notion to Obsidian

7
By  Parth Shah

What I particularly appreciate is that AFFiNE doesn't force you to use all its features at once. You can treat it like a simple note-taking app, creating documents and organizing them into folders, or take things a step further with tags, collections, and its infinite canvas. Everything is there when you need it, without making the basic act of taking notes feel unnecessarily complicated.

Unlike Notion, where I've often found myself spending more time building the perfect workspace than actually using it, AFFiNE makes it easy to start with a simple collection of notes and gradually introduce more advanced features as I need them. That said, I won't go as far as to claim that there's no learning curve at all and that you'll immediately know your way around every feature. Some of its more advanced tools still take a little getting used to, but for everyday note-taking, I've found AFFiNE considerably easier to get the hang of.

AFFiNE makes visual brainstorming part of my workflow

My whiteboard finally lives alongside my notes

The problem with using Notion, Obsidian, and Google Keep wasn't that any of these apps were inherently bad. It was more that my workflow was split across different apps, largely because my reasons for using each of them were different. Similarly, whenever I need to annotate something, sketch out an idea, or jot down handwritten notes, I'll often find myself turning to Goodnotes or Apple Notes, even when I'm working on my MacBook. So, while I might technically be using three apps for note-taking, the number of apps I actually rely on is considerably higher.

This is another area where AFFiNE has made my life easier. Its built-in infinite canvas, appropriately called Edgeless mode, lets me draw, annotate, and visually organize my ideas without needing to switch to a completely different app. There's a freehand drawing tool, along with shapes, arrows, sticky notes, and plenty of other elements you can add to the canvas. I can even bring existing documents into the mix, which makes it particularly useful when I'm researching an article or trying to make sense of a complicated topic.

You can also use the canvas to create mind maps, which is something I'd previously turn to tools like XMind or NotebookLM for. Being able to do all of this within the same workspace where I'm already taking notes means I have one less reason to constantly jump between applications.

AFFiNE is completely free for personal use

I've tried more note-taking apps over the years than I'd like to admit, and while plenty of them have impressed me, very few have managed to stick around for long. AFFiNE, though, has managed to earn itself a permanent spot in my workflow. It's not necessarily that it does everything better than Notion, Obsidian, or Google Keep, but rather that it brings the features I regularly use across all three into one place.

The cherry on top is that AFFiNE's core note-taking features are completely free to use. You get unlimited local workspaces, document editing, and access to its infinite canvas without paying a dime. The free plan even includes 10 GB of cloud storage, which is more than enough for my needs.

Of course, there are paid plans if you need more storage, support for larger files, or additional collaboration features, but I haven't felt the need to upgrade. There's also an optional AI add-on, but that's not something I'm particularly interested in paying for.

item.title: I ran DLSS 5 on Rockstar’s GTA trilogy, and GTA 6 suddenly doesn’t feel that far ahead
item.itunes:title: I ran DLSS 5 on Rockstar’s GTA trilogy, and GTA 6 suddenly doesn’t feel that far ahead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's been 13 years since the last Grand Theft Auto title came out, and after countless delays, leaks, and hitches, the next one is finally getting bigger on the horizon.

A lot has changed since 2013. Modern GPUs render games faster, "generate" frames when they need to, and most recently, make games look life-like. GPUs have been slowly moving inch-by-inch towards photorealistic graphics for years, but DLSS 5 was the landmark moment where it all seemed to get real, literally and figuratively.

I've tested GTA 5 with neural rendering before, but curious to see how the same technique would hold up on remasters of games released over twenty years ago, I decided to give it another pass. GTA 6 may arrive in 30 days, but I'm convinced we've arrived at photorealistic gaming before it.

GTA III

The first 3D GTA ever somehow gets neural rendering

I'd forgive anyone for mistaking one of these images for a photograph pulled from the internet, because a singular neural pass from DLSS 5, injected into the game through a ReShade add-on called Deep Fried Chicken (yes, really) is doing more for Liberty City's faces and streets than decades of texture mods ever managed. As you can see, DLSS 5's neural rendering layer is doing some extraordinary things to faces in GTA III which have never quite looked human.

GTA III isn't a game you'd ever find me playing. The first GTA game I ever experienced was San Andreas, and even that was four years after its polished PC release came out. Liberty City isn't a place I have much nostalgia for, as such. And yet, during my testing, all it took was the first thirty minutes of gameplay to make me want more of it.

The characters looked as though they belonged in the world around them, the map felt inhabited and animated, and the city itself felt like a place that you find a home in, much more than a categorical GTA-styled sandbox where you blow things up for fun and watch the chaos ensue. Neural rendering undoubtedly gave Liberty City a sense of "life" that I would've never thought a game that came out in 2001 could have in 2026, and that's highly ironic for an AI feature. Yet, here we are.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

GTA San Andreas

Grove Street, home, like the way I remember it

GTA San Andreas was the GTA that I grew up with, the one I spent countless hours on, the reason why I know the lyrics to Toto's Hold the Line by heart, and if I ever get lost without a map in Los Angeles, the reason why I'd probably be fine.

It's also the reason why I was heartbroken to not find Las Venturas and San Fierro in GTA V. Not that it kept me from playing the story mode seventeen times anyway, but the absence of the two cities always made it seem like San Andreas had a hole that could not be filled. Seeing those two cities rendered in the Definitive Edition with DLSS 5 was liberating in a way that, I finally knew what it would have felt had they been a part of the newer game.

As for the visuals, I could probably talk from dusk till dawn. Everything was visually striking, from reflectivity on the panels of cars, the way the water behaves, to the way the Hydra cuts through the sky in bad weather. The Definitive Edition feels worthy of its name, albeit with DLSS 5 doing much of the heavy-lifting. If there's a way to revisit San Andreas and preserve even a little of what Grove Street felt like to me when I was eight, neural rendering would be it.

Stop calling it AI slop — upscaling is democratizing high-end gaming for the 99%

Better visuals for those not on the bleeding edge.

26
By  Samarveer Singh

GTA Vice City

Suddenly, the new Vice City has a lot to live up to

What GTA San Andreas is to me, Vice City is to plenty of other gamers who grew up with Rockstar's games, and I have no doubts about that, because I know quite a few personally. I got to experience it first on an Nvidia GT 610, and the only thing I understood about the game at that age was that you had to steal cars. Grand Theft Auto, quite literally.

Vice City was a visually funny game. Tommy Vercetti sprinted funnily, could die from stepping into a puddle of still water, and the world around him was already jagged before 2002's consumer GPUs made it jagged-er still. It had a charm the sharpest edges couldn't ruin, which was a good thing, because the edges themselves were plentiful.

Watching this world through DLSS 5 is a pleasure through the eyes of a fan. When it rains, car headlights now paint puddles, neon transforms the ambience in a way that the original game engine was reaching for but could never, and the sunrise on the beach filled the sky with the kind of orange that I find it jarring to associate with a game that came out decades ago. Tommy Vercetti went from a character to a person, which is something he deserved just as much as Claude from GTA III.

Maybe DLSS 5 isn't so bad after all

Over the past few months, I've watched and, dare say, learned a lot from the online discourse surrounding artistic intent versus neural rendering, which are often presented as at odds with one another. But when I look at the game worlds that are more than 20 years old be transformed and brought to life through this technology in a way that it makes me want to revisit them more than I have in years, I'm led to believe that perhaps there is a right balance to be found after all. And maybe, just maybe there's a way that it's doing more for preservation than the remasters meant for exactly that purpose.

item.title: The Zelda: The Wind Waker HD PC port I've always wanted is finally here, complete with buttery-smooth 60fps
item.itunes:title: The Zelda: The Wind Waker HD PC port I've always wanted is finally here, complete with buttery-smooth 60fps
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Thanks to AI, the number of very unofficial retro and modern game PC ports dropping right now is through the roof. Recent examples include PC ports of The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening, a Mac port of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, and even a PC port of the Pokémon: Let's Go games.

One port that recently caught my attention is ZeldaWWHDRecomp, a static recompilation of the Wii U's The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker HD for Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android. With so many recompilations releasing these days, it's tough to tell what games are total AI slop and which are solid, AI-assisted static recompilations. After all, if a recompilation sucks, you're better off just emulating whatever game you're trying to play.

Thankfully, ZeldaWWHDRecomp is pretty solid, though it's far from perfect. The recompilation's main draw over emulating the Wii U classic with Cemu is mod support and 60fps through interpolation (there's an experimental true 60fps mode, but it doesn't run well right now), a substantial jump over the original game's 30fps. In my experience, The Wind Waker HD runs very smoothly on my ROG Xbox Ally X20, though I get occasional stutters when shaders compile as I enter new areas. Thankfully, updates over the past week have made this issue less frequent.

I don't need the Switch 2's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake — I already made my own

Ship of Harkinian powers a native PC port of the N64 classic.

16
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Watch Toon Link slice-and-dice enemies at 60fps

Mod support adds fan-made quests to The Wind Waker HD

While Zelda: The Wind Waker HD runs silkily-smooth for the most part, seeing Toon Link's timeless art style at 60fps is a bit jarring at first. Thankfully, I quickly got used to the fluid motion, and I don't think I could go back now. Everything from running to swinging Link's sword looks impressively smooth and far more modern, running at a higher frame rate.

Mod support adds extra features like fan-made story quests, including extra Treasure Charts, a Story Notebook, and quest mods that appear in the Rito postboxes you'll find throughout the game's world. All of these mods are optional and can be turned off in the game's menu if you want a more authentic experience.

Other quality-of-life upgrades include save states, internal resolution scaling up to 3840x2160 (I played at 1920x1080), picture scaling, and controller-specific button prompts. In my case, I used Xbox buttons, which show up in the game's UI, and switched them to By Label to make the controls less confusing on the ROG Xbox Ally X20. You can also change joystick deadzones, open the Wii U's GamePad screen in a separate window, and even turn on HDR (The Wind Waker HD looks incredible with high-dynamic range on).

Like all recompilations, ZeldaWWHDRecomp doesn't include any The Wind Waker HD Wii U game files. This means you need to supply your own dump of the game's disc image, or acquire it elsewhere. Once you supply your own game files, the setup process translates The Wind Waker HD's PowerPC code into C and compiles it for your system.

You can even import The Wind Waker HD save files from Cemu, which I really appreciated since I'm already several dungeons deep in the game through the popular emulator. That said, it takes a bit of work to hunt down the save files on Windows 11. It's also worth mentioning that updates for ZeldaWWHDRecomp drop almost daily, so if you're running into stability issues, keep an eye on the project's GitHub page.

I manage all the decompilations and recompilations I play through Quiver, a port-focused Windows 11 launcher that makes it easier to track what you have installed and update the games in your library.

Zelda: The Wind Waker has aged remarkably well

The art style that divided fans in 2002 looks incredible today

Back in 2002, at 13, I was just too cool for The Wind Waker's cel-shaded graphics. I was out here playing super mature games like Halo: Combat Evolved and Oddworld: Munch's Odyssey, and I had no time for kiddie games like The Wind Waker. Adding to that vibe at the time, the game's cartoony visual style felt like a slap in the face to fans after the realistic-looking Zelda Space World demo in 2000.

Fast-forward to 2026, and The Wind Waker still looks absolutely stunning, especially the 2013 HD Wii U remaster this static recompilation ports over to PC, while games like The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess, a darker, grittier entry in the series that was a direct response to the Toon Link backlash, just looks okay to me now. That said, the recent Dusklight Twilight Princess PC port includes an option to remove the bloom Twilight Princess is known for, which cleans up its blown-out visuals a lot.

I wouldn't go so far as to say that ZeldaWWHDRecomp is the definitive way to play The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker since the game still runs a bit more reliably when emulated in Cemu, but if the team behind the project can iron out some of its shader loading issues, I can see that changing, mainly due to the native PC port's 60fps support. With the Ocarina of Time remake just around the corner, now is a great time to dive back into one of the long-running series' best entries.

I don't think Nintendo will ever beat this unofficial Zelda: Twilight Princess port

Dusklight is a very impressive PC, Android, Linux and Mac port of The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess.

Thanks to AI, the number of very unofficial retro and modern game PC ports dropping right now is through the roof. Recent examples include PC ports of The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening, a Mac port of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, and even a PC port of the Pokémon: Let's Go games.

One port that recently caught my attention is ZeldaWWHDRecomp, a static recompilation of the Wii U's The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker HD for Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android. With so many recompilations releasing these days, it's tough to tell what games are total AI slop and which are solid, AI-assisted static recompilations. After all, if a recompilation sucks, you're better off just emulating whatever game you're trying to play.

Thankfully, ZeldaWWHDRecomp is pretty solid, though it's far from perfect. The recompilation's main draw over emulating the Wii U classic with Cemu is mod support and 60fps through interpolation (there's an experimental true 60fps mode, but it doesn't run well right now), a substantial jump over the original game's 30fps. In my experience, The Wind Waker HD runs very smoothly on my ROG Xbox Ally X20, though I get occasional stutters when shaders compile as I enter new areas. Thankfully, updates over the past week have made this issue less frequent.

I don't need the Switch 2's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake — I already made my own

Ship of Harkinian powers a native PC port of the N64 classic.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Watch Toon Link slice-and-dice enemies at 60fps

Mod support adds fan-made quests to The Wind Waker HD

While Zelda: The Wind Waker HD runs silkily-smooth for the most part, seeing Toon Link's timeless art style at 60fps is a bit jarring at first. Thankfully, I quickly got used to the fluid motion, and I don't think I could go back now. Everything from running to swinging Link's sword looks impressively smooth and far more modern, running at a higher frame rate.

Mod support adds extra features like fan-made story quests, including extra Treasure Charts, a Story Notebook, and quest mods that appear in the Rito postboxes you'll find throughout the game's world. All of these mods are optional and can be turned off in the game's menu if you want a more authentic experience.

Other quality-of-life upgrades include save states, internal resolution scaling up to 3840x2160 (I played at 1920x1080), picture scaling, and controller-specific button prompts. In my case, I used Xbox buttons, which show up in the game's UI, and switched them to By Label to make the controls less confusing on the ROG Xbox Ally X20. You can also change joystick deadzones, open the Wii U's GamePad screen in a separate window, and even turn on HDR (The Wind Waker HD looks incredible with high-dynamic range on).

Like all recompilations, ZeldaWWHDRecomp doesn't include any The Wind Waker HD Wii U game files. This means you need to supply your own dump of the game's disc image, or acquire it elsewhere. Once you supply your own game files, the setup process translates The Wind Waker HD's PowerPC code into C and compiles it for your system.

You can even import The Wind Waker HD save files from Cemu, which I really appreciated since I'm already several dungeons deep in the game through the popular emulator. That said, it takes a bit of work to hunt down the save files on Windows 11. It's also worth mentioning that updates for ZeldaWWHDRecomp drop almost daily, so if you're running into stability issues, keep an eye on the project's GitHub page.

I manage all the decompilations and recompilations I play through Quiver, a port-focused Windows 11 launcher that makes it easier to track what you have installed and update the games in your library.

Zelda: The Wind Waker has aged remarkably well

The art style that divided fans in 2002 looks incredible today

Back in 2002, at 13, I was just too cool for The Wind Waker's cel-shaded graphics. I was out here playing super mature games like Halo: Combat Evolved and Oddworld: Munch's Odyssey, and I had no time for kiddie games like The Wind Waker. Adding to that vibe at the time, the game's cartoony visual style felt like a slap in the face to fans after the realistic-looking Zelda Space World demo in 2000.

Fast-forward to 2026, and The Wind Waker still looks absolutely stunning, especially the 2013 HD Wii U remaster this static recompilation ports over to PC, while games like The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess, a darker, grittier entry in the series that was a direct response to the Toon Link backlash, just looks okay to me now. That said, the recent Dusklight Twilight Princess PC port includes an option to remove the bloom Twilight Princess is known for, which cleans up its blown-out visuals a lot.

I wouldn't go so far as to say that ZeldaWWHDRecomp is the definitive way to play The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker since the game still runs a bit more reliably when emulated in Cemu, but if the team behind the project can iron out some of its shader loading issues, I can see that changing, mainly due to the native PC port's 60fps support. With the Ocarina of Time remake just around the corner, now is a great time to dive back into one of the long-running series' best entries.

item.title: I uninstalled my GPU's RGB software, and the stutter I'd blamed on drivers went with it
item.itunes:title: I uninstalled my GPU's RGB software, and the stutter I'd blamed on drivers went with it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Sometimes, with PC gaming, your high-end rig can pull solid frame rates, yet every few seconds the screen can hitch or stutter during fast motion, ruining your gameplay. When this happens to me, my first thought is blaming drivers, a faulty Windows update, or bad shader compilation, which leads to hours of Display Driver Uninstaller wipes, clean reinstalls, and BIOS tweaks.

For me, the actual source of the frame drops wasn't my graphics card or the drivers. It was, in fact, the bloated, poorly optimized vendor utility suite running invisible polling threads in the background. PC optimization isn't just about tweaking core clocks; it's about eliminating software bloat. By purging invasive GPU and motherboard RGB utilities, you can wipe out mysterious background stutters and restore true frame time consistency.

I let the NVIDIA App overclock my GPU, and it left me impressed

For a "conservative" OC tool, the NVIDIA App gave me remarkable results

7
By  Samarveer Singh

There's a lot of overhead

Your game is stuttering for a reason

Consumer hardware lighting and monitoring suites have a lot of hidden overhead. This means that RGB software can destroy frame times. This is down to the constant WMI and SM bus polling. To synchronize colors across fans, coolers, and GPUs, software suites constantly poll hardware registers via Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and the system management bus (SM bus). Every few milliseconds, these background threads interrupt the CPU and saturate system buses.

You also get DPC latency spikes. Poorly written vendor services cause deferred procedural latency spikes. This means when a background lighting daemon locks up system resources to update an LED color, it can delay high-priority hardware interrupts, causing micro-stuttering and audio crackling during games.

This is what I noticed most, even though my frames looked consistent when I checked averages. I could feel constant micro-stuttering, especially when there was a lot of movement on screen.

How to get SignalRGB set up

This open-source software is lighter

If you're running a poorly optimized render utility suite like Armory Crate, RGB Fusion, or Dragon Center, luckily there is a clean, lightweight open-source control alternative. By swapping out these proprietary bloats for lean open alternatives, you can restore your performance.

Fan favorites and my personal go-to are OpenRGB and Signal RGB. By switching to a unified open-source ecosystem that communicates cleanly with hardware without running heavy, resource-hogging background telemetry and web frameworks, you keep full control without sacrificing performance.

The great thing about these suites is that they also come with set-and-forget hardware profiles. You can leverage onboard memory on modern GPUs and peripherals to save hardware loading profiles directly to the device, letting you completely disable the background software runner when you don't need it.

In order to strip out your software bloat, the first thing you need to do is actually identify the culprit. You can do this by checking Task Manager for resource-hungry background services tied to your GPU manufacturer or motherboard brand, like lighting services, ASUS Control Center, or RGB engines.

Once you've found it it's time to save the profiles and uninstall. Set a static color profile via your onboard hardware if that's supported. Then completely uninstall the vendor utility suite using a robust uninstaller so that you can wipe residual registry entries. You can relocate fan control and critical fan curves into your motherboard BIOS or use lightweight tools like Fan Control and then use an open-source utility like OpenRGB if you still want basic lighting control without the baggage. If you don't, you can leave the static color profile you set before uninstalling so you don't need any of the fuss whatsoever.

Lastly, you can benchmark and verify. Fire up your favorite demanding title and notice how the mysterious micro-stutters have vanished.

You might not have all the features you want

But the performance you get is worth it

It's worth noting that you lose some hardware control features by removing your GPU and motherboard utility programs; despite being invasive, they provide a level of control you might not get from open source and BIOS settings.

For example, uninstalling a massive utility suite often means losing custom fan curves or a hardware monitoring dashboard, forcing you to move fan control into the BIOS, which might not save your presets and might not offer as much control as the accompanying software.

You might also lose complex cloud sync and rainbow wave effects, since Signal RGB and OpenRGB don't offer as many lighting customization options. For me, realistically, it felt like my gaming performance and system responsiveness took major priority over a glowing desk, but this might not be the case for everyone.

Reclaim your performance

This fix is simple

We spend countless hours chasing ghost problems in GPU driver settings when the real enemy is sitting right in our Windows startup tray. Stripping out unnecessary background load is one of the easiest ways to reclaim your frame rates. Ditch the heavy RGB software suites, clean up your background processes, and get back to enjoying stutter-free gaming.

item.title: I remapped the Copilot key on my keyboard to open my local model instead
item.itunes:title: I remapped the Copilot key on my keyboard to open my local model instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Microsoft Copilot hasn't got the best rep. What was designed to be a convenient feature to make AI more accessible for those less tech-savvy, it actually turned into something many (myself included) loathed. What's more is my current laptop, the trusty Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 9, a Copilot+ PC with a Snapdragon X Elite CPU, is primed for running local models. With PowerToys and a little tinkering, I managed to make this dedicated Copilot button on my keyboard more useful by loading a local LLM.

The problem with Microsoft Copilot

It's not really local is it?

The dedicated button on my laptop's keyboard was enticing to me. No matter which app I was using, I could press this key and fire up a local instance, utilizing the excellent capabilities of the included chip. Boy, was I wrong. All this thing does is launch Microsoft's Copilot app. So far, so good. But this is entirely cloud-based. What's the difference between running ChatGPT, Claude, or some other cloud-based solution? Many of us already pay for one such service.

That's where the Copilot implementation started to fall apart for me. The laptop in question has that mighty Snapdragon X Elite processor, based on Arm and rocking an integrated NPU that can actually perform. This Qualcomm Hexagon NPU is rated at 45 TOPS, which means very little, so I wanted to put it to the test with a locally hosted LLM. The model I have has just 16GB of RAM, so we won't be going wild, but even a small yet useful model can work wonders.

I pitted local AI against Claude Pro by actually doing the math — and the winner wasn't straightforward

Which trade-offs are you more comfortable with?

2
By  Tanveer Singh

I already made good use of Ollama and LM Studio on other devices, and it was something I toyed with on this very laptop, so I never found myself using Copilot at all. The Deepseek-r1 model is brilliant, notably 8b. The same goes for Qwen3.5 with both 4b and 9b options. For testing, I opted for qwen3.5:4b. It easily fits inside the constraints of the 16GB RAM. I don't tend to have long-winded conversations, so context windows won't be a problem, but it also means I can actually have other apps running on the laptop.

That's the entire point of this experiment. To launch an LLM window with the single keystroke, allowing me to expand horizons while handling other tasks. Having a beefy model that soaks up all the RAM and page file would defeat the purpose and slow things down to a halt.

Why running local AI is important to me

I'm a firm believer we should run LLMs on local hardware, be it the device you're actively using or on a specific device within a home lab. Keeping prompts, replies, and processing all on hardware you own ensures you maintain control over everything. It's similar to why I prefer to store all my files on a NAS. I trust my LAN more than Google, Apple, Microsoft, and other big tech giants. The same goes for LLMs and other agents, and I'd much prefer to rely on open-weight models without remote inference.

Saving money, no additional subscriptions. It sounds like the ideal AI implementation, and having it just one keystroke away should be brilliant.

I ran a local LLM entirely off a NAS, and it turned my storage box into an AI-hosting workstation

Edge LLMs and embedding models perform well even on NAS CPUs

By  Ayush Pande

Changing the Copilot key with PowerToys

Creating my own local AI hotkey

PowerToys is a free tool available for Windows. This handy collection of tools allows for the OS to be customized beyond what the traditional control panel offers. All that was required was for Keyboard Manager to be enabled and then create a new remap for the shortcut tool. This was then linked to LM Studio, so every time the key is pressed, the app opens, and I'm good to go with a fully local version of Qwen. After saving everything, I tested the keystroke, and it worked.

Instead of opening Copilot, the AI key now fired up LM Studio, loading qwen3.5:4b. Interestingly, there's a small delay with Copilot and the same is experienced with LM Studio as the model reserves enough RAM. It's only for the first prompt and is something I grew used to with self-hosting Open WebUI with the same occurrence. The only drawback with PowerToys is the app needs to be running for the remap to be effective. If I don't want it to run in the background, Copilot once again starts up.

Why not just change it within the Settings app? The only choice I see when setting the shortcut key is Copilot. No LM Studio or anything else.

The local AI is useful, but it doesn't beat cloud

Nothing really stands against flagship models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. It's why we're struggling with GPUs, memory, and tech availability and pricing in general. These companies are hoarding all these important components to ensure their cloud-based models have ample resources to handle prompts in record time. Firing up Claude or ChatGPT will see almost instant responses with reasoning, thinking, and external tools used. It's impressive.

The same cannot be said for my local Qwen model running in LM Studio on the Lenovo Snapdragon Copilot+ PC. The 16GB of RAM is a limiting factor. It's also standard laptop memory, which doesn't have the best bandwidth for running AI. A GPU would be better, but even then it still pales in comparison to what's available with cloud LLMs. It all boils down to what's expected from the models and how one interacts with them.

Microsoft should alter the Copilot key

This single shortcut should be configurable. I'm still questioning the motives behind making a dedicated AI key tied to Microsoft's own Copilot, cloud-based AI. I get it; it's Microsoft, and the company wants you to use their offering, but it's not really Microsoft AI. Yes, the company is developing its own LLM, but it's based on OpenAI's GPT. If you've used ChatGPT, Copilot feels very similar. And like ChatGPT, Microsoft offers a freemium model with its Copilot implementation.

AI is increasingly becoming a category of software instead of one simple app. The way we're using AI and interacting with these tools is continuing to evolve, and a move like this isn't necessarily about rejecting Microsoft's Copilot but instead allowing me to decide how I want to go about using AI on my own Windows PC. My Lenovo laptop shipped with a dedicated Copilot key, but pressing it now opens the AI assistant I actually want to use. This is how it should have been in the first place.

NotebookLM's best features are coming to Microsoft Copilot soon

Copilot might finally become useful.

It's not really local is it?

No matter which app I was using, I could press this key and fire up a local instance, utilizing the excellent capabilities of the included chip. Boy, was I wrong. Many of us already pay for one such service.

That's where the Copilot implementation started to fall apart for me. The laptop in question has that mighty Snapdragon X Elite processor, based on Arm and rocking an integrated NPU that can actually perform. I'm a firm believer we should run LLMs on local hardware, be it the device you're actively using or on a specific device within a home lab. item.title: Used Wi-Fi 6 routers are still a better home networking deal than Wi-Fi 7 routers for most homes
item.itunes:title: Used Wi-Fi 6 routers are still a better home networking deal than Wi-Fi 7 routers for most homes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Buying a Wi-Fi 7 router is often the home networking upgrade many households default to. It has been marketed as the one-stop solution to all your Wi-Fi woes, and the newest standard ought to improve your Wi-Fi, right? Well, it turns out most people can't really make use of a Wi-Fi 7 router. Whether it's their house's Ethernet infrastructure, internet plan speed, or device compatibility, most of Wi-Fi 7's promises simply fall flat.

Instead of buying an expensive Wi-Fi 7 router that does nothing for your home network, I suggest buying one or more Wi-Fi 6 routers on the used market. By repurposing them as wired access points or for short Ethernet runs, you can improve your home network without wasting money.

Replacing my ISP's router was the single biggest upgrade I made to my home network

It made a bigger difference than changing any router settings I had access to

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Extend your wireless coverage without extenders or a mesh network

Wi-Fi 6 routers make great access points

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Besides an increase in the theoretical bandwidth, a Wi-Fi 7 router can bring improved coverage, latency, and congestion management to a home network. The great thing is that most homes can achieve the same thing by adding a used Wi-Fi 6 router to their existing network. No matter how good your router is, you probably have one or more dead zones in the house. And with too many smart devices on the network, latency is unavoidable.

A Wi-Fi 6 router repurposed as a wired access point can instantly eliminate chronic dead zones in your house. As long as you can connect its WAN port to your main router's LAN port with, say, a Cat6 cable, you can create a strong, secondary access point for your wireless devices. You just need to factory reset the used router, put it into bridge mode, disable DHCP to avoid conflicts, assign it an IP address outside your DHCP pool, and use the same SSID and password as your main router.

By hardwiring your main router to the used router, you turn the latter into a wireless broadcaster that doesn't have the downsides of a wireless extender. Plus, you don't need to buy an expensive mesh network just for a single dead zone; one or two used routers are enough. You can find pre-owned Asus, MSI, and TP-Link Wi-Fi 6 routers on eBay for as low as $10–$15, whereas a decent mesh system will cost around $100.

Alternatively, you can reserve the used Wi-Fi 6 router for your smart home network, keeping it 2.4GHz–only. This will prevent your smart home from dragging down your main network. If the Wi-Fi 6 model you're buying is no longer supported by the manufacturer, you can flash it with custom firmware to continue receiving security updates.

Don't throw away your old router! Here's how I repurposed mine
8
By  Rich Edmonds

Bring Ethernet closer to your high-performance devices

Easier to manage and a godsend for reliability

If you've been struggling with Wi-Fi latency or coverage issues on your smart TV, streaming box, or gaming console, a used Wi-Fi 6 router can be just what you need. Instead of routing a long Ethernet cable from your main router to your latency-sensitive devices, you can hardwire it to a Wi-Fi 6 router sitting close by, and then add another wired link to your TV or console.

By doing so, you avoid the hassle and cost associated with long Ethernet runs, and replace them with short, manageable runs that are easier to hide along the floor or ceiling — no routing through walls. Your TV, console, or other devices get a reliable wired connection, and your wireless devices get to enjoy a cleaner, congestion-free Wi-Fi network. You can even bring secondary desktop PCs to the LAN using your newly acquired access point.

Why I insist on Ethernet on my PC even when it's a pain to set up

Ethernet beats Wi-Fi hands down, and is worth a few hassles

36
By  Tanveer Singh

Used Wi-Fi 6 routers are way cheaper than Wi-Fi 7 models

It's not comparable at all

I touched upon the affordability of pre-owned Wi-Fi 6 routers in contrast to expensive mesh systems, but what about a new Wi-Fi 7 router? While a used Wi-Fi 6 router may cost you up to $25, a proper tri-band Wi-Fi 7 model will typically sit close to $200. Occasional deals can drop the investment to around $170, but that's still way more expensive than a Wi-Fi 6 model sourced from eBay.

Wi-Fi 7 models haven't been on the pre-owned market long enough, so you'll still have to shell out around $100 for a used model. It makes no sense to invest in a Wi-Fi 7 router simply for extra coverage and modern features that your devices can't even use. Wi-Fi 7 made a lot of noise about MLO and 320 MHz channels, but neither enjoys widespread support. Besides, wider channels only help you close to the router; they increase interference away from it.

Eventually, your devices will start leveraging Wi-Fi 7 features fully, but it may be time for Wi-Fi 8 by then. In any case, you don't need to worry about missing out on Wi-Fi 7 for a few more years. Most households aren't subscribed to multi-gig plans or have home servers that demand a high-end Wi-Fi 7 router. A used Wi-Fi 6 router could be enough to patch the holes in your Wi-Fi network.

One of Wi-Fi 7's best features can actually slow your connection down

MLO is why Wi-Fi 7's speeds look incredible on paper, but real-world numbers are a bit more complicated

1
By  Ty Sherback

Buying used routers may not be your first instinct, but it's worth it

For many people, buying a router is a one-time expense that lasts for years with no additional cost. That said, spending $200 on a Wi-Fi 7 router still doesn't make sense if it makes no improvement to your network. If a used Wi-Fi 6 router can significantly boost your Wi-Fi and wired networks for under $25, it deserves to be considered.

item.title: The Lucy AI Studio brings AI agents, local models, and private storage together
item.itunes:title: The Lucy AI Studio brings AI agents, local models, and private storage together
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Everyone’s using AI these days, but despite powerful desktop hardware being readily available, almost all of that AI usage happens remotely in faraway data centers. This is a potential privacy issue, since you’re sharing personal data with someone else’s AI, and you’re at the mercy of the reliability and security of something beyond your control.

AI isn’t the only thing we rely on the cloud for, either. Cloud file storage is almost a necessity, with recurring monthly fees to store your personal files in data centers owned by massive corporations. Even our smart home systems aren’t actually all that smart. The real “brains” of smart home devices, once again, are mostly in the cloud. None of it runs locally.

However, people everywhere are pushing back against this. As a result, local AI models are becoming increasingly popular. Home NAS (Network-Attached Storage) devices are flying off the shelves, and smart home systems, like Home Assistant, keep all the processing in-house.

Cephalon's Lucy AI Studio is attempting to bring these two worlds together. It's a compact desktop computer designed to serve as your personal AI powerhouse, private cloud, and intelligent assistant, all in one device.

Lucy AI Studio is more than just an AI PC or a NAS

Cephalon Lucy AI Studio
Brand
Cephalon
Storage
Variable
CPU
Ai Ryzen Max (Various)
Memory
Up to 192GB
Operating System
Linux/Lucy AIOS

The Cephalon Lucy AI Studio is a specialized computer designed for local AI processing, offline smart home control, and high-speed NAS functionality. This could be the heart of your home network.

See at Cephalon

Of course, you can already run AI models on hardware you can buy off the shelf or that you already own. What makes the Lucy AI Studio different is that it combines multiple distinct devices into one central system that can sit at the heart of your home network. Instead of managing separate systems for local AI and storage, you’ll have one dedicated home for your AI agents, models, and data.

Because your AI models, photographs, videos, documents, and everything else live on the same machine, you’ll get local AI access and use that data for whatever you need. For example, Lucy can help you find relevant information across your project files, analyze documents and images, turn those insights into reports or other useful content, and save the results back to your original folders — all within your local computing environment, accessible from devices on your home network.

Cephalon is pioneering a language-based approach to file management, where AI can understand the contents of your files rather than relying on mere filenames and directory structures.

The Lucy AI Studio makes AI part of your personal home computing environment, and you’re always in control.

There's some serious hardware behind the local AI promise

Credit: Cephalon

If you know anything about running local AI models, you also know that it takes sophisticated hardware to do anything useful.

There are three planned versions of the Lucy AI Studio, offering different balances of capability and budget: Pro, Max, and Ultra. All three models have the same basic template and feature set, but significantly different performance levels.

The Max is particularly interesting for AI enthusiasts. It uses AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 processor, which offers 16 CPU cores, 32 threads, and integrated Radeon 8060S graphics with 40 compute units. There's also an AMD XDNA 2 neural processing unit, with the system offering up to 126 TOPS of combined AI performance.

What really makes the difference here is the 128GB of unified memory, with up to 96GB available for dynamic allocation to the GPU. That leaves lots of room for modern cutting-edge AI models. Memory capacity, rather than raw processing power, is the main limit to local AI. Even the most powerful consumer GPUs, which would otherwise have performed well with these AI models, simply don’t have enough memory to run them.

For those who need even more headroom, the Ultra steps up to a Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 with 192GB of unified memory and up to 144GB available for GPU allocation.

The more affordable Pro uses an AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS with 32GB of DDR5 RAM, making it an entry point into the Lucy ecosystem.

All three versions include five SATA drive bays and can support up to 100TB of total storage, depending on the drives installed. That's a huge amount of space for documents, photographs, videos, AI models, datasets, and backups. The Max and Ultra also include 10Gb Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity. Even the entry-level Pro gets Wi-Fi 7 and two 2.5Gb Ethernet connections.

Each Lucy configuration is designed for different model sizes and workloads, including vision-language models, speech processing, and LLMs, so buyers should choose the configuration that best matches their intended use.

Hermes Agent makes Lucy more than a machine that answers questions

Credit: Cephalon

AI models that wait for your input to do their thing are great, but AI really reaches its potential when you go agentic. AI agents keep pursuing the goals you give them, and don’t require your input to work.

To this end, Lucy AI Studio is integrated with Hermes Agent. Developed by Nous Research, Hermes Agent provides an agent framework that can interact with local files and execute workflows locally. That’s the ideal solution for an AI-capable computer that’s also your NAS.

Lucy comes configured to use Hermes with local models, but you can also connect supported cloud models when you need additional capabilities or faster responses. It’s seamless hybridization, adapting to your needs.

Hermes offers an intuitive interface beyond a web-based dashboard. You can use your existing chat apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, and Signal. This means you can send instructions to Hermes from wherever you are, as long as you have access to your chat apps.

But Lucy supports a broad range of AI tools. If you want to use OpenClaw, Codex, or Claude Code, you can freely throw them into the mix. That makes Lucy one of the best investments a home-based software developer can make.

From AI-generated content to coding, Lucy is designed for real workflows

The Cephalon Lucy AI Studio isn’t just aimed at AI tinkerers and early adopters. This is a powerful computer system for people who want to do real work for real use cases. It’s designed to empower creators, developers, and enthusiasts who want to make AI a useful part of daily life.

The system includes access to ComfyUI, a popular node-based environment for generative AI workflows.

Using ComfyUI, Lucy AI Studio supports local AI video generation at resolutions up to 768p and durations of up to 15 seconds. For faster generation, users can choose a recommended five-second, 480p workflow using a four-step “Turbo” setting.

For higher-resolution output, generated videos can also be upscaled to 2K using third-party online tools. While higher-quality local generation requires additional processing time, running the core video-generation workflow on Lucy gives creators another option alongside cloud-based generation services. Because generation happens locally, you're not bound by the content restrictions imposed by cloud AI platforms, giving you much more creative freedom.

While Lucy runs Ubuntu right now, Cephalon is working on Lucy AIOS, a customized, agent-first operating environment based on Omarchy. Eligible early Lucy buyers will receive the Lucy AIOS upgrade at no additional charge when it becomes available.

Here’s how to get in on the ground floor with the Cephalon Lucy AI Studio

Cephalon plans to launch Lucy AI Studio through Kickstarter, with limited super early-bird prices starting at $799 for the Pro, $2,799 for the Max, and $3,799 for the Ultra.

The respective MSRPs are $899, $3,999, and $4,999. As with any crowdfunded hardware project, pricing, delivery schedules, and software availability are subject to change, so keep a close eye out for updates. Interested in having your AI agents, models, and data in one dedicated workspace? Follow Lucy AI Studio on Kickstarter to get notified when the campaign launches.

This is a potential privacy issue, since you’re sharing personal data with someone else’s AI, and you’re at the mercy of the reliability and security of something beyond your control.

AI isn’t the only thing we rely on the cloud for, either. Cloud file storage is almost a necessity, with recurring monthly fees to store your personal files in data centers owned by massive corporations. Even our smart home systems aren’t actually all that smart. The real “brains” of smart home devices, once again, are mostly in the cloud. None of it runs locally.

However, people everywhere are pushing back against this. As a result, local AI models are becoming increasingly popular. Home NAS (Network-Attached Storage) devices are flying off the shelves, and smart home systems, like Home Assistant, keep all the processing in-house.

Cephalon's Lucy AI Studio is attempting to bring these two worlds together. It's a compact desktop computer designed to serve as your personal AI powerhouse, private cloud, and intelligent assistant, all in one device.

The Cephalon Lucy AI Studio is a specialized computer designed for local AI processing, offline smart home control, and high-speed NAS functionality. This could be the heart of your home network.

See at Cephalon

Of course, you can already run AI models on hardware you can buy off the shelf or that you already own. What makes the Lucy AI Studio different is that it combines multiple distinct devices into one central system that can sit at the heart of your home network. Instead of managing separate systems for local AI and storage, you’ll have one dedicated home for your AI agents, models, and data.

Because your AI models, photographs, videos, documents, and everything else live on the same machine, you’ll get local AI access and use that data for whatever you need. For example, Lucy can help you find relevant information across your project files, analyze documents and images, turn those insights into reports or other useful content, and save the results back to your original folders — all within your local computing environment, accessible from devices on your home network.

Cephalon is pioneering a language-based approach to file management, where AI can understand the contents of your files rather than relying on mere filenames and directory structures.

The Lucy AI Studio makes AI part of your personal home computing environment, and you’re always in control.

There's some serious hardware behind the local AI promise

Credit: Cephalon

If you know anything about running local AI models, you also know that it takes sophisticated hardware to do anything useful.

There are three planned versions of the Lucy AI Studio, offering different balances of capability and budget: Pro, Max, and Ultra. All three models have the same basic template and feature set, but significantly different performance levels.

The Max is particularly interesting for AI enthusiasts. It uses AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 processor, which offers 16 CPU cores, 32 threads, and integrated Radeon 8060S graphics with 40 compute units. There's also an AMD XDNA 2 neural processing unit, with the system offering up to 126 TOPS of combined AI performance.

What really makes the difference here is the 128GB of unified memory, with up to 96GB available for dynamic allocation to the GPU. That leaves lots of room for modern cutting-edge AI models. Memory capacity, rather than raw processing power, is the main limit to local AI. Even the most powerful consumer GPUs, which would otherwise have performed well with these AI models, simply don’t have enough memory to run them.

For those who need even more headroom, the Ultra steps up to a Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 with 192GB of unified memory and up to 144GB available for GPU allocation.

The more affordable Pro uses an AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS with 32GB of DDR5 RAM, making it an entry point into the Lucy ecosystem.

All three versions include five SATA drive bays and can support up to 100TB of total storage, depending on the drives installed. That's a huge amount of space for documents, photographs, videos, AI models, datasets, and backups. The Max and Ultra also include 10Gb Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity. Even the entry-level Pro gets Wi-Fi 7 and two 2.5Gb Ethernet connections.

Each Lucy configuration is designed for different model sizes and workloads, including vision-language models, speech processing, and LLMs, so buyers should choose the configuration that best matches their intended use.

Hermes Agent makes Lucy more than a machine that answers questions

Credit: Cephalon

AI models that wait for your input to do their thing are great, but AI really reaches its potential when you go agentic. AI agents keep pursuing the goals you give them, and don’t require your input to work.

To this end, Lucy AI Studio is integrated with Hermes Agent. Developed by Nous Research, Hermes Agent provides an agent framework that can interact with local files and execute workflows locally. That’s the ideal solution for an AI-capable computer that’s also your NAS.

Lucy comes configured to use Hermes with local models, but you can also connect supported cloud models when you need additional capabilities or faster responses. It’s seamless hybridization, adapting to your needs.

Hermes offers an intuitive interface beyond a web-based dashboard. You can use your existing chat apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, and Signal. This means you can send instructions to Hermes from wherever you are, as long as you have access to your chat apps.

But Lucy supports a broad range of AI tools. If you want to use OpenClaw, Codex, or Claude Code, you can freely throw them into the mix. That makes Lucy one of the best investments a home-based software developer can make.

From AI-generated content to coding, Lucy is designed for real workflows

The Cephalon Lucy AI Studio isn’t just aimed at AI tinkerers and early adopters. This is a powerful computer system for people who want to do real work for real use cases. It’s designed to empower creators, developers, and enthusiasts who want to make AI a useful part of daily life.

The system includes access to ComfyUI, a popular node-based environment for generative AI workflows.

Using ComfyUI, Lucy AI Studio supports local AI video generation at resolutions up to 768p and durations of up to 15 seconds. For faster generation, users can choose a recommended five-second, 480p workflow using a four-step “Turbo” setting.

For higher-resolution output, generated videos can also be upscaled to 2K using third-party online tools. While higher-quality local generation requires additional processing time, running the core video-generation workflow on Lucy gives creators another option alongside cloud-based generation services. Because generation happens locally, you're not bound by the content restrictions imposed by cloud AI platforms, giving you much more creative freedom.

While Lucy runs Ubuntu right now, Cephalon is working on Lucy AIOS, a customized, agent-first operating environment based on Omarchy. Eligible early Lucy buyers will receive the Lucy AIOS upgrade at no additional charge when it becomes available.

Here’s how to get in on the ground floor with the Cephalon Lucy AI Studio

Cephalon plans to launch Lucy AI Studio through Kickstarter, with limited super early-bird prices starting at $799 for the Pro, $2,799 for the Max, and $3,799 for the Ultra.

The respective MSRPs are $899, $3,999, and $4,999. As with any crowdfunded hardware project, pricing, delivery schedules, and software availability are subject to change, so keep a close eye out for updates. Interested in having your AI agents, models, and data in one dedicated workspace? Follow Lucy AI Studio on Kickstarter to get notified when the campaign launches.
